title: Spray Painting and Sanding Nano-Enabled Paint
summary: Paints with nano titanium dioxide can put nanoparticles into the air when you spray or sand them. NIOSH believes this nanomaterial might harm workers. Capture dust at the source, use a respirator, and protect your eyes, skin, and hearing.
talking_points: Nano titanium dioxide is a common nanomaterial in paint. NIOSH believes it might be harmful because it causes lung damage and cancer in lab animals, and NIOSH has a recommended exposure limit for it.
OSHA has no specific standard for engineered nanomaterials, but other standards, such as respiratory protection and hazard communication, may apply.
Ask your employer whether the paint is nano-enabled. Check the label and safety data sheet, and CPWR's inventory at nano.elcosh.org. The information is often missing.
Connect your orbital sander to a vacuum with a HEPA filter to capture dust before it gets in the air. Otherwise use the dust bag that came with the sander.
Use a respirator for spray mist and sanding dust. Your employer must provide the right type through a full respiratory protection program. N95 or P100 filters effectively capture nanomaterials.
Work upwind when you spray, and rotate painters to reduce exposure.
Wear goggles or a face shield, gloves, and disposable clothing when spray painting.
Wear hearing protection when using an orbital sander.
site_hazards_to_check: Airless spraying with no ventilation or respirator
Co-workers who sand dried paint near other workers
Painting products with no information about nanomaterials
